candidateRows: Psychophysical harmony is substantially more expected on theism than on naturalism and therefore supports theism over naturalism.
This is the opening formulation of the likelihood comparison that directly answers the debate motion and structures Cutter's subsequent case.
After defining psychophysical harmony, Cutter states its proposed evidential significance while limiting the immediate comparison to theism and naturalism.
Actual psychophysical laws are not merely antecedently improbable but specially valuable because they provide consciousness and enable major consciousness-involving goods.
The move identifies the special, value-laden character of the observed arrangement, supplying the evidential datum rather than relying on improbability alone.
Following examples of alternative psychophysical laws, Cutter distinguishes bare improbability from specialness and argues that most alternatives would eliminate important goods.
Pain exhibits normative harmony because its badness and reasons for avoidance align with its actual functional association with avoidance behavior.
Normative harmony is one of the principal data offered for the motion, and the pain example specifies both the datum and contrasting disharmonious possibilities.
Cutter introduces normative and semantic harmony, then focuses on how pain's evaluative role matches its behavioral role unlike inversion or neutral-experience worlds.
Evolution does not explain psychophysical harmony because it either leaves altered experience mappings causally irrelevant or presupposes pain's harmonious link to avoidance.
This move blocks a major naturalistic explanation of the central datum across both causally closed and interactionist accounts of consciousness.
Cutter considers causal closure and interactionism, arguing that swapping experiential roles preserves physical evolution and that ordinary evolutionary explanations assume the alignment at issue.
Psychophysical harmony is unlikely on naturalism because most possible mappings, including especially simple mappings, would not produce comparable goods or harmony.
This supplies the naturalism side of the central likelihood ratio and answers the concern that a prior preference for simple laws favors harmonious mappings.
After recapping the harmony data, Cutter argues that naturalism does not predict them and that zombie, particle-experience, and grayscale laws remain simpler alternatives.
Psychophysical harmony is comparatively likely on theism because a perfectly good creator would be expected to realize valuable states enabled by harmonious laws.
The move provides the theistic half of the likelihood comparison by connecting divine goodness with the consciousness-involving goods made possible by the actual laws.
Having argued that harmony is unlikely on naturalism, Cutter contrasts theism, under which a good and powerful creator has reason to realize valuable conscious goods.
If pain experiences are identical with neural events, no psychophysical correlation requires explanation, so the harmony argument does not affect identity naturalism.
This is Oppy's principal objection: identity eliminates the distinct correlated items presupposed by the argument and thereby insulates his preferred naturalism from it.
Cutter's claim that harmonious links between conscious and physical or functional roles favor theism over naturalism.
Oppy argues that pain and neural occurrences are one event, analogizes the case to two names for Venus, and says Cutter's argument excludes his preferred view.
Pain's causal and rationalizing relation to aversive behavior is known a priori, making pleasure-pain inversion inconceivable rather than a genuine epistemic alternative.
The move attacks the alternative mappings used to establish improbability by denying that a central inversion scenario belongs to a relevant space of possibilities.
Cutter's use of conceivable pleasure-pain inversions and broad epistemic possibility to argue that actual harmony is antecedently unlikely.
Oppy claims pain unlike pleasure necessarily causes and rationalizes avoidance, then rejects mere consistency with first-order logic as an interesting standard of possibility.
Given naturalistic identity theory, the probability of psychophysical harmony is one, contrary to the likelihood premise required by the theistic argument.
This directly contradicts the pro side's core likelihood comparison by assigning certainty, rather than low probability, to harmony conditional on identity naturalism.
Cutter's central claim that the observed psychophysical harmony is much less likely on naturalism than it is on theism.
Near the end of his opening, Oppy applies his identity account to the probabilistic formulation and contends that it changes the relevant calculation decisively.
Identity theory does not defeat the argument because the official claim concerns epistemic likelihood rather than explanation, and type-B identity retains the relevant epistemic gap.
This is Cutter's principal reply to Oppy's central defense, reformulating the case to survive identities and locating its force in epistemic rather than ontological dependence.
Oppy's contention that phenomenal-neural identity removes any correlation question and makes harmony certain on his naturalistic theory.
Cutter concedes identities do not themselves demand explanation, distinguishes the official probabilistic argument, and asks whether Oppy's materialism allows an epistemic physical-phenomenal gap.
Whether zombies are epistemically possible depends on the correct constraints on epistemic possibility, and stronger a priori constraints may make zombies inconceivable.
This bears directly on whether Oppy's identity naturalism has the epistemic gap that Cutter needs in order to extend the harmony argument to physicalism.
Cutter's challenge that Oppy must say whether physical zombies are coherently conceivable despite being metaphysically impossible.
Oppy firmly denies metaphysical zombie possibility but questions the governing notion of epistemic possibility, suggesting that sufficiently strong a priori constraints could also exclude zombies.
Type B physicalism leaves the same epistemic possibility space for psychophysical correlations as dualism, so it does not undermine the claim that harmony is unlikely on naturalism.
This is a direct defense of the harmony argument against identity naturalism, explaining why necessary psychophysical identities do not raise the epistemic likelihood of harmony.
Oppy's uncertainty about zombie conceivability and whether his identity view contains the epistemic gap assumed by Cutter's argument.

Cutter distinguishes type A from type B physicalism, concedes that the argument does not address type A, and argues that type B retains an epistemic gap across which harmonious identities remain antecedently unlikely.
A probability distribution formed from total ignorance lacks a principled shape, especially over an infinite space, so such imagined priors do not clearly bear on agents' actual credences.
The objection attacks the probabilistic foundation for claiming that harmonious psychophysical connections are unlikely on naturalism before relevant empirical evidence is included.
Cutter's claim that metaphysical necessity leaves intact a prior credence distribution over epistemically possible psychophysical correlations.

Using possible electron values, Oppy argues that stripping away all evidence leaves no justified distribution: a flat distribution fails over an infinite range, while any non-flat distribution appears arbitrary.

Meaningful comparative likelihood judgments can be justified from sparse backgrounds, as illustrated by Bayesian arguments that apparently pointless suffering is more likely on naturalism than on theism.
This supplies a methodological defense of the sparse-background likelihood comparisons on which the psychophysical harmony argument depends.
Oppy's objection that total ignorance supplies no principled probability distribution and has no clear normative relation to actual credences.

Cutter contends that comparative probabilities need not include the evidence being assessed in their background and argues that familiar evidential arguments from suffering show such abstraction can remain intelligible and justified.
Explanatory comparison of complete theories is preferable to Bayesian likelihood assignments, because theoretical commitments and fit can be assessed without dubious sparse-background probabilities.
This offers an alternative framework for comparing theism and naturalism that challenges the necessity and legitimacy of the Bayesian machinery used by the harmony argument.
Cutter's appeal to Bayesian arguments from evil as evidence that sparse-background comparative likelihood judgments can be legitimate.

Oppy proposes asking how rival theories explain suffering, including the extra commitments theistic explanations may require, and treating simplicity and explanatory performance as the relevant comparative considerations.

Probability legitimately applies to fine-tuning when an indeterministic process supplies outcomes and chances, but probability over merely epistemically entertained cosmological models lacks an evident measure.
The distinction clarifies that Oppy's criticism is not a blanket rejection of probability but a targeted concern about measures over hypothesis spaces like those used in harmony reasoning.
Cutter's question whether Oppy's worries would also make probabilistic fine-tuning comparisons between design and non-design illegitimate.

Oppy accepts chance-based reasoning where a physical phase transition defines possible outcomes, while withholding acceptance where physicists' possible universe-models lack a clear probability measure.
Epistemic probabilities can manage ignorance in constrained cases, but without objective chances or a sufficiently specified setup their applicability remains problematic.
This refines the probability objection by distinguishing rationally constrained ignorance from ungrounded assignments, a distinction directly relevant to priors over psychophysical laws.
The question whether justified epistemic probability claims remain available when no physical process supplies objective chances for the alternatives.

Oppy uses fair dice to show that rational constraints can support probabilities without quantum indeterminism, then separates genuine causal chance from probabilities used merely to manage ignorance in deterministic settings.
Subjective probabilities do not solve the problem when competing fundamental theories provide no information from which to assign even prior comparative numbers.
The move applies Oppy's general concern specifically to theory comparison, maintaining that calling the probabilities subjective does not establish a rational likelihood ordering.
Cutter's suggestion that the harmony argument uses probabilities to codify ignorance about psychophysical correlations under naturalism and theism.

Oppy allows that subjective probability may sometimes be coherent but argues that a priori comparison of major physical theories illustrates cases where there is simply nothing available to ground numerical assignments.
Comparative likelihoods can be clearly ordered without precise numbers or a uniquely natural measure, so measure-theoretic difficulties need not defeat the evidential force of harmony.
This directly defends the central likelihood comparison of the harmony argument against Oppy's claim that absent a privileged measure there is no justified probabilistic assessment.
Oppy's claim that comparisons of fundamental theories may provide no basis for assigning prior probabilities, even when those probabilities are labeled subjective.

Cutter argues from message-like leaves and a hypothetical scriptural inscription inside every atom that overwhelming comparative evidence can be recognizable despite unknown numerical likelihoods, infinite spaces, and measure-selection problems.
When simplicity and fit with the data both favor one hypothesis, dominance can settle the comparison without numerical probabilities, leaving the Bayesian formulation with no substantive work to do.

The response accommodates Cutter's ordinal comparisons while arguing that they support a non-Bayesian theory-choice framework rather than vindicating the probability machinery of the harmony argument.
Cutter's argument that comparative likelihoods can strongly favor theism even without exact values or a uniquely privileged probability measure.
Oppy grants that ratio or dominance reasoning can avoid exact numbers, but concludes that the real work is then performed by simplicity and fit with evidence rather than by Bayesian formalism itself.
The obvious causal role of pain in avoidance behavior does not make their separation inconceivable or a priori epistemically impossible.
This directly defends the contingency needed by the harmony argument against the claim that pain and avoidance are necessarily connected.
The earlier claim that pain necessarily causes and rationalizes avoidance behavior, thereby explaining their correlation.
Brian distinguishes obvious empirical truths from a priori necessities, invokes epiphenomenalism and Cartesian skeptical scenarios, and denies an a priori link between experience and bodily behavior.
Possessing the concept of pain may itself require experiences that make pain's connection with avoidance behavior evident.
The move challenges Cutter's appeal to conceivable separation by arguing that competent possession of the pain concept may already disclose its behavioral connection.
Cutter's contention that pain can be conceived independently of physical avoidance behavior.

Graham argues that a priori knowledge requires the relevant concept, that acquiring the pain concept plausibly requires experiencing pain, and that such experience may reveal its avoidance connection.
Cartesian and radical-dream scenarios coherently separate painful experience from actual bodily avoidance behavior.
These scenarios supply the principal conceivability case for denying a necessary psychophysical connection between pain and physical avoidance behavior.
Oppy's suggestion that acquiring the concept of pain may entail knowing its connection to avoidance behavior.

Cutter argues that a Cartesian subject could acquire a phenomenal pain concept while lacking a body, then develops dream cases in which pain occurs without corresponding physical behavior or dispositions.
The necessary claim connecting pain with aversive behavior is generic rather than universal and therefore permits exceptional cases.
This qualification preserves Oppy's proposed necessary pain-behavior connection while accommodating the exceptional scenarios introduced by Cutter.
Cutter's dream and Cartesian cases involving pain without actual physical avoidance behavior.
Oppy explains that his original claim was deliberately generic: pain normally causes and rationalizes aversive behavior across possible worlds even though individual worlds may contain outliers.
Recombining copies of an admitted pain-without-avoidance outlier yields a possible world in which even the generic connection is false.
The recombination argument targets Oppy's revised generic necessity directly and attempts to generate a counterexample world rather than merely an isolated exception.
Oppy's claim that a necessary generic pain-avoidance connection can consistently admit occasional outlier cases.
Cutter proposes populating a world entirely with intrinsic duplicates of an outlier who feels pain without avoidance, producing a world where the generic generalization itself fails.
Cutter's recombination argument depends on a substantive patchwork principle for epistemically possible worlds that requires independent justification.
The move isolates the modal principle underwriting Cutter's counterexample and challenges whether epistemic possibilities may be freely recombined in the required way.
Cutter's construction of a world containing only copies of pain-without-avoidance outliers.
Oppy observes that Cutter appears committed to looseness-and-separateness or patchwork principles under which components of epistemically possible worlds may be freely combined.
Qualified recombination principles plausibly govern epistemic possibility because coherently imaginable scenarios can be assembled from independently conceivable parts.
This supplies the modal premise needed for Cutter's recombination counterexample to Oppy's proposed necessary generic connection.
Oppy's challenge concerning whether patchwork principles legitimately apply to epistemically possible worlds.
Cutter endorses qualified patchwork principles for epistemic possibility, notes that unrestricted formulations may create paradoxes, and asks whether Oppy rejects even the epistemic version.
A naturally encoded striking message in a possibly contingent constant would support both that constant's contingency and theism, analogously to psychophysical harmony.
The analogy explains how striking structure can jointly provide evidence for contingency and divine selection even when necessity initially remains a serious hypothesis.
The preceding thought experiment proposing that an encoded message in pi could favor theism plus contingency.

Cutter rejects pi as an ideal example because its digits may contain every finite sequence, substitutes a naturally translated constant of nature, and links its middle-ground modal status to psychophysical laws.
Hypothetical evidence ruled out by one's theory raises a distinct question from the actual evidence available for rational belief revision.
This challenges the argumentative force of merely possible spectacular evidence by separating counterfactual belief-change scenarios from assessment of the evidence actually possessed.
The proposal that sufficiently striking psychophysical or encoded structure could overturn an initial commitment to necessity.
Oppy asks how a theorist should treat evidence that is not merely absent but impossible on the theory, and what doxastic obligations attach to evidence the theorist expects never to receive.
Observed disharmony does not defeat the argument because actual psychophysical laws need only be far more value-producing than chance, not maximally harmonious.
This directly answers the closing objection that irrationality and mismatched mental states undermine the evidential comparison on which the harmony argument relies.
The objection that pervasive irrationality and psychophysical disharmony may erase the claimed probabilistic advantage for theism.
Cutter compares imperfect harmony to an imperfect poem produced by a monkey, then argues that reallocating conscious states may merely relocate mismatches among experience, belief, and behavior.
Holding all physical facts fixed, no alternative assignment of experiences is clearly more psychophysically harmonious than the actual assignment.
The claim directly rebuts an objection from imperfect rationality by distinguishing improvements to the physical world from improvements in psychophysical assignment.
The contrary suggestion that people or the world could display substantially greater psychophysical harmony than they actually do.

After discussing irrational beliefs and behavior, Cutter clarifies that greater harmony is possible through different physical facts but denies a clearly superior experiential assignment under fixed physical facts.
Strongly reductive accounts of consciousness diminish the harmony argument, though an epistemic gap between physical and phenomenal facts may preserve a version of it.
This closing concession identifies the principal condition under which the argument loses force and the epistemic distinction Cutter invokes to retain it.
Oppy's reductive identity-naturalist position that removes an independent phenomenal assignment requiring explanation.
In his closing statement, Cutter grants substantial force to the reductive objection while maintaining that epistemic possibility may sustain the argument despite metaphysical identity claims.
If consciousness is irreducible, psychophysical laws and correlations present striking facts that are substantially less surprising on theism than on naturalism.
The proposition states the debate's core comparative case for psychophysical harmony as evidence favoring theism, conditional on irreducible consciousness.
Cutter concludes that the harmony argument proceeds straightforwardly for those who independently regard consciousness as irreducible, because the observed correlations favor theism comparatively.
The reductive-materialist objection is not uniquely naturalistic because some theists also accept reductive materialism and inherit the same concern.
The qualification limits the proposed theism-naturalism contrast by locating the decisive disagreement in theories of consciousness rather than theology alone.
Cutter's closing presentation of irreducible consciousness as the setting in which psychophysical harmony comparatively favors theism.
Oppy accepts the broad closing summary but adds that reductive theories cross the theist-naturalist divide, so his objection can also arise within theism.
